sources.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case - CNBC
passages: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.

That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."

extraction.body: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company guilty of misleading consumers about the privacy of their data a decade ago. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew said in the order. New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the decision could be the largest verdict by a single state against the company. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," he said in a press conference after the ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and ‌protect our ⁠consumers," he added. However, the company's stock has not reacted negatively to the development. Meta shares were climbing 1.77% and clocked in above $706.5 a piece at 3:01 p.m. ET. It is likely that the company will appeal the ruling so the decision doesn't have a direct impact in its finances. The case in question is related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, with the trial showing that the British consulting firm harvested data from close to 90 million Facebook users without their consent through a third-party app. New Mexico was also at the helm of a landmark case against Meta and centered on social media addiction. The company was accused of misrepresenting the impact of its platforms on the mental health of children. The company ended up settling and agreed to make several changes to its apps, including daily usage limits and "nighttime blocks" for teenagers, as well as "enhanced age assurance measures" that would prevent children from using them. Parents and guardians would have additional tools as well. According to the lawsuit, Meta "developed and refined a set of psychologically manipulative platform features designed to maximize young users' time spent on its social media platforms." New Mexico and other states pointed to features including infinite scroll, autoplay, and likes as examples of mechanisms they say encourage prolonged and compulsive use. The attorneys general also allege Meta knew its platforms could contribute to anxiety, depression and suicide among some young users but presented its products as safe.

extraction.body: Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."

Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.

In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.

"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.

Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

passages: Meta Platforms has been ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a judge ruled that Facebook misled consumers for years about how it handled their personal information, delivering one of the largest financial penalties against a company in US history.The ruling, issued on Wednesday, followed a jury verdict finding that Facebook violated New Mexico's consumer protection law nearly 44 million times.

On a $25 billion balance, that equates to $3.75 billion in interest over one year, before any compounding.The latest penalty substantially exceeds the $5 billion charge imposed on Facebook by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over privacy violations.

The case centred on the social media platform's representations about data privacy, third-party access to user information, and its handling of harmful content.Judge Francis Mathew said Facebook's communications formed part of a deliberate strategy to mislead the public.

However, jurors rejected some of the state's claims, including allegations that the company made false statements about removing harmful content.Meta Plans to Appeal the JudgmentMeta's chief legal officer, CJ Mahoney, criticised the ruling and the state attorney general's approach to the case. 'This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,' Mahoney said in a statement, according to CBS News.He also argued that the lawsuit sought to impose a penalty on speech by enforcing new rules governing what people could say online.

passages: Tesla said Wednesday it will start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year, even as federal regulators investigate whether the vehicle meets vehicle safety standards .
The gold-hued, autonomous two-seater lacks a steering wheel and other traditional controls.
During the company's third-quarter earnings call, Lars Moravy, vice president of engineering at Tesla, said the Cybercabs produced today are all destined for the company's own robotaxi fleet.
The company will scale as it learns about delivery, ownership, and fleet management of autonomous vehicles, Moravy added.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

Cybercabs, unlike Tesla's other vehicles, don't come with steering wheels and brake pedals.

Elon Musk admitted during the call, however, that "the vast majority" Cybercabs will be "essentially Tesla-owned" and will be under its ride service operations.

Lars Moravy, VP of engineering at the company, said that the automaker is "trying to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of this year, 2026," during its third quarter earnings calls. Moravy added that Tesla is already manufacturing Cybercabs at its Gigafactory in Texas, but those are meant for its internal robotaxi fleet. If the company does succeed in getting the vehicles to customers this year, it will start small. The company first unveiled the Cybercab back in 2024, but it wasn't until September this year that it started offering rides on it through its Robotaxi app in Austin, Texas. Tesla has also just started taking inquiries for those interested in buying units. Specifically, it's looking for entities who can help "build its robotaxi network," indicating that it'll initially sell them to companies that can purchase whole fleets. Cybercabs, unlike Tesla's other vehicles, don't come with steering wheels and brake pedals. It cannot be driven by a human driver and relies on the company's Full Self-Driving software. At the moment, Tesla owners can only get the Supervised version of the suite, which still requires a human driver behind the wheel. Ashok Elluswamy, Director of AI at Tesla, said during the call that the company believes it can start switching on Unsupervised Full Self-Driving on "some of the first customer vehicles to be part of the Robotaxi fleet" around the second quarter of 2027. It's worth noting that shortly after Tesla started offering Cybercab rides in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) launched a probe into the vehicles. The agency said that the company self-certified that the vehicles are compliant with all relevant Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS). It plans to look into the process and data the automaker used to self-certify to determine whether the vehicles do indeed adhere to those standards.

coreStoryFacts.text: Tesla said Wednesday it will start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year, even as federal regulators investigate whether the vehicle meets vehicle safety standards .
The gold-hued, autonomous two-seater lacks a steering wheel and other traditional controls.
During the company's third-quarter earnings call, Lars Moravy, vice president of engineering at Tesla, said the Cybercabs produced today are all destined for the company's own robotaxi fleet.
The company will scale as it learns about delivery, ownership, and fleet management of autonomous vehicles, Moravy added.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Tesla first floated the idea of selling the autonomous vehicle to third parties last month around its Cybercab event in Austin and even posted a form for people interested in buying robotaxis.
But it wasn't clear if Tesla would follow through, or how.

Current regulations don't accommodate vehicles without manual controls, though the Department of Transportation recently proposed removing those requirements for vehicles that are designed to be autonomously driven.
In the meantime, NHTSA said it would investigate the Cybercab to "examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues."
There is at least one obstacle that could throw off Tesla's Cybercab fleet plans.
The outcome of that investigation could affect whether Tesla, or anyone else, can legally operate the Cybercab.
"But, you know, the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transported as a service."

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has talked for years about building a massive fleet of low-cost robotaxis, but until recently, those plans centered on turning privately owned Tesla vehicles into self-driving taxis with a software update.
Today, Tesla owners can subscribe to Full Self-Driving (Supervised), an advanced driver-assistance system that automates many driving tasks but still requires the driver to take control.

The company continues to push out software updates to the system to improve its capabilities, but a human driver is still required to remain engaged and ready to take over — even though many videos show drivers testing the limits of that rule.
Automakers traditionally self-certify whether their vehicles comply with FMVSS rules, and Tesla did the same.
Tesla is aiming to start selling Cybercabs to customers before the year ends.
The company first unveiled the Cybercab back in 2024, but it wasn't until September this year that it started offering rides on it through its Robotaxi app in Austin, Texas.
Tesla has also just started taking inquiries for those interested in buying units.
Cybercabs, unlike Tesla's other vehicles, don't come with steering wheels and brake pedals.
Since the Unsupervised version of Tesla's Full Self-Driving suite isn't available to consumers yet, the first Cybercabs sold to customers can't be added to the Tesla's ride-hailing fleet yet.
Moravy added that Tesla is already manufacturing Cybercabs at its Gigafactory in Texas, but those are meant for its internal robotaxi fleet.
As it learns about "ownership and fleet management of autonomous vehicles in customer hands," Moravy said, Tesla will scale up Cybercab's sales.
Elon Musk admitted during the call, however, that "the vast majority" Cybercabs will be "essentially Tesla-owned" and will be under its ride service operations.

sources.title: OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft - CNBC
passages: OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year.
Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips.
Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively.
All three report quarterly results next week.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google.
Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT.
Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems.
In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property.
The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models .
Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.
"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers.
That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.

Alongside the Cloud deployment, GPT models will appear in the Google Antigravity client.
Until now, Antigravity has supported Google’s Gemini as well as Claude.
Google recently rolled out Gemini 4 Argon across its AI footprint, bringing its flagship AI back to parity with the competition—at least if you ask Google.
It does seem like an improvement over Gemini 3.1 Pro, but it burns through tokens at an astonishing rate.
Anthropic’s Claude models are already supported in Google Cloud, but the OpenAI deal will offer another alternative to Gemini for those not feeling the Argon love.
Google says it’s now the only large cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed LLMs.
Google would certainly prefer that everyone used its Gemini models with Google Cloud services, but soon, you’ll have more options.
While OpenAI notes that Microsoft continues to be its primary cloud partner, the full suite of current GPT 6 and 6.1 models—Astra, Sol, and Luna—will launch on Google Cloud.

coreStoryFacts.text: OpenAI and Google have yet to confirm exactly which GPT models will be coming to Cloud and Antigravity, but it stands to reason that GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol may be included.

OpenAI says that “Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via the model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace.” This enables enterprise customers with “spend commitments” through Google Cloud to use OpenAI’s models if they choose.
Also confirmed in today’s announcement is that OpenAI models are coming to Google’s Antigravity tool, as well as Gemini Agent.

Like Cloud’s model garden, Antigravity already supports Anthropic models including Claude Opus & Sonnet 4.6 for free/Plus/trial accounts (until November 2), with Opus & Sonnet 5.5 models available to paid subscribers on Pro and higher tiers.
OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year.
Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips.
Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42% , respectively.
All three report quarterly results next week.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google.
Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT.
Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems.
In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property.
The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models .
Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.
"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers.
That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.
Bringing GPT models to Google Cloud could be a big deal for enterprise, but even individual users could see some benefit from the deal.
Alongside the Cloud deployment, GPT models will appear in the Google Antigravity client.
Until now, Antigravity has supported Google’s Gemini as well as Claude.
Google recently rolled out Gemini 4 Argon across its AI footprint, bringing its flagship AI back to parity with the competition—at least if you ask Google.

passages: OpenAI's GPT models are heading to Google Cloud "in the coming weeks," and will also arrive in Google's Antigravity tool and Gemini Agent, under a deal between the two companies, according to 9to5Google. The details came in an announcement on Wednesday.

OpenAI said Google Cloud customers will be able to buy its frontier models through the model garden, with purchases handled through the Google Cloud Marketplace. That matters most to enterprise customers who already have spend commitments with Google Cloud, because they can use those commitments to pay for OpenAI's models if they choose.

Google Cloud's model garden already offers Anthropic's Claude models alongside open models and Google's own Gemini family. Google said it is focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can pick the right one for each job and keep costs down.

The announcement also confirms that OpenAI's models are coming to Google's Antigravity tool and to Gemini Agent. Antigravity already supports Anthropic models, which are available on free, Plus and trial accounts for a limited period and on higher tiers for paid subscribers.
OpenAI and Google have yet to confirm exactly which GPT models will come to Cloud and Antigravity. OpenAI described the timing for Antigravity as "soon," compared with "the coming weeks" for Cloud.

For businesses the practical effect is convenience. A team that has standardized on Google Cloud will be able to try models from three major labs without signing a separate contract and billing arrangement with each one.

But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention. He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders. “Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping. Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content. Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said. Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay. Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales. “On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.” Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year. “We expect to make money from Muse by taking a small fee from transactions,” Zuckerberg said at the event.

The proposed model would allow Meta to earn revenue when users purchase products or services through the app, potentially creating a new commercial opportunity beyond the advertising business that has traditionally driven the company’s earnings.

However, the app’s rapid adoption has also brought renewed attention to concerns about consumer trust and the handling of personal information, particularly given the extent of access an AI assistant may require to perform tasks effectively.
Kate Winick, a principal analyst at Forrester, identified consumer confidence as a critical factor that could influence the long-term success of Meta’s AI ambitions.
“The more information Muse has, the more effective it can be, and overall trust in Meta remains low,” Winick said.

She argued that Meta had developed a business model in which users continued engaging with its products despite persistent concerns about data privacy, provided the services delivered sufficient convenience and value.

“But Meta has cultivated a reputation that negates trust as a condition for engagement: consumers almost expect to have their data mismanaged in exchange for a high level of connectivity and utility, and have shown that they're willing to keep showing up as long as the product experience delivers,” she added.

Winick’s remarks underscore the challenge facing Meta as it expands AI services that may depend on access to personal preferences, communications and other information to deliver useful, tailored responses.

The company’s ability to persuade users to trust Muse with such information could prove important as it seeks to turn the application’s early popularity into sustained engagement and commercial growth.

The developments also come amid renewed scrutiny of Meta’s data protection practices. Earlier on Wednesday, a judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25 billion after a jury found that it had misled consumers about its handling of personal data and failed to adequately address misinformation on Facebook.

The judgment adds to the legal challenges facing the technology company over its treatment of user information, even as it promotes new AI products designed to provide more personalised digital experiences.

While Muse’s first-month performance offers Meta an early indication of consumer demand for personal AI assistants, the company faces the dual task of converting that interest into sustainable revenue while addressing questions about privacy and public confidence.

For Zuckerberg, the app’s growing user base and shopping activity represent an early opportunity to demonstrate the commercial potential of Meta’s AI investments, although its longer-term prospects will depend on whether users continue to find the service useful and are comfortable entrusting it with more of their digital lives.

extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is “entering a new phase” focused on scaling and monetisation, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on October 21, as the social media giant looks to turn early user growth into a significant revenue driver. Muse, which launched in early September , has attracted more than 10 million users in the United States and Canada in the past month and a half. About 25 percent of the people who have set up Muse use it daily with shopping being the most common use case, Zuckerberg said. "With an average purchase size of over $200, Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before, and in the first week we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected," Zuckerberg said during the company's earnings conference call. Beyond shopping, he said other popular use cases for Muse include personal productivity tasks and connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. Now that Muse has “clear product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta is focusing on scaling the AI agent, growing revenue, and optimising its compute costs as the company looks to roll out the product to billions of its users. "We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together. So we’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible," he said. The Muse network would allow users’ AI agents to interact and work with those of their friends and family, alongside enterprise applications. Notably, Zuckerberg said he expects Muse to generate higher revenue per user over time than the several hundred dollars Meta currently earns annually from each American user of its existing family of apps who also uses Muse. "This will take some time, but we’re starting to work on this now," he said. Last month, Zuckerberg described Muse as the centrepiece of Meta’s AI strategy , saying he expects the agent to evolve into a personal superintelligence used by billions of people worldwide. The Meta chief said the firm would pursue monetisation on Muse "sooner than its normal playbook", given the scale of the costs involved and the potential opportunity. Meta would build commerce tools to earn fees on transactions facilitated by Muse, paid by businesses. Subscriptions would be another key revenue stream, with users able to pay for access to advanced AI models and additional tokens, while business owners and companies could subscribe to features tailored to growing their operations or using Muse at work. "Making a version of Muse that people can bring into different corporate environments and work there, we think, is going to be a big deal," Zuckerberg said. Last month, Meta brought together its paid subscription offerings under a single brand, Meta One , and started rolling out subscription bundles to users globally. Meta One now has 15 million subscribers. Since Muse is very compute intensive to run, Meta is also building out capacity to expand the AI agent to more than a billion users over the next few years. "We expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale," Zuckerberg said. "If compute efficiency continues improving quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years," he added. Meta narrowed its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 to $135 billion to $145 billion , from its prior range of $130 billion to $145 billion. Muse central to business model of smart glasses Muse is also central to Meta’s plan to build a software and superintelligence business around its smart glasses, which Zuckerberg said are priced to keep hardware profits low. He expects growing sales and paid subscriptions to significantly improve the business’s profitability. Overall, Meta's revenues rose 26 percent year-on-year to $64.6 billion while net profit increased 264 percent to $9.86 billion. Yesterday, a US state court judge ruled that Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The social media giant said it is also creating a new class of non-voting shares with an effective date of January 2027, to help fund its massive AI spending. The move would help the company finance potential acquisitions and attract top talent without diluting voting control of Zuckerberg or other shareholders. "The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said.

"We believe that Muse will make you money," Zuckerberg told the room full of developers.
"And we are standing behind this by making Muse free for a huge number of tokens with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions."
Wall Street analysts are high on Meta's Muse agent, with Wells Fargo and KeyBanc Capital Markets raising their price targets on Meta amid early uptake of the app.

The app's early success sent Meta stock soaring 11% on Monday , as the market digested the positive news.

Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content. Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year. He expects growing sales and paid subscriptions to significantly improve the business’s profitability.
Meta would build commerce tools to earn fees on transactions facilitated by Muse, paid by businesses.

Subscriptions would be another key revenue stream, with users able to pay for access to advanced AI models and additional tokens, while business owners and companies could subscribe to features tailored to growing their operations or using Muse at work.
"Making a version of Muse that people can bring into different corporate environments and work there, we think, is going to be a big deal," Zuckerberg said.

"The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said.
The move would help the company finance potential acquisitions and attract top talent without diluting voting control of Zuckerberg or other shareholders.

extraction.body: Meta’s personal AI agent Muse is “entering a new phase” focused on scaling and monetisation, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on October 21, as the social media giant looks to turn early user growth into a significant revenue driver. Muse, which launched in early September , has attracted more than 10 million users in the United States and Canada in the past month and a half. About 25 percent of the people who have set up Muse use it daily with shopping being the most common use case, Zuckerberg said. "With an average purchase size of over $200, Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before, and in the first week we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected," Zuckerberg said during the company's earnings conference call. Beyond shopping, he said other popular use cases for Muse include personal productivity tasks and connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. Now that Muse has “clear product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta is focusing on scaling the AI agent, growing revenue, and optimising its compute costs as the company looks to roll out the product to billions of its users. "We think that billions of Muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together. So we’d like to create a large-scale Muse network as quickly as possible," he said. The Muse network would allow users’ AI agents to interact and work with those of their friends and family, alongside enterprise applications. Notably, Zuckerberg said he expects Muse to generate higher revenue per user over time than the several hundred dollars Meta currently earns annually from each American user of its existing family of apps who also uses Muse. "This will take some time, but we’re starting to work on this now," he said. Last month, Zuckerberg described Muse as the centrepiece of Meta’s AI strategy , saying he expects the agent to evolve into a personal superintelligence used by billions of people worldwide. The Meta chief said the firm would pursue monetisation on Muse "sooner than its normal playbook", given the scale of the costs involved and the potential opportunity. Meta would build commerce tools to earn fees on transactions facilitated by Muse, paid by businesses. Subscriptions would be another key revenue stream, with users able to pay for access to advanced AI models and additional tokens, while business owners and companies could subscribe to features tailored to growing their operations or using Muse at work. "Making a version of Muse that people can bring into different corporate environments and work there, we think, is going to be a big deal," Zuckerberg said. Last month, Meta brought together its paid subscription offerings under a single brand, Meta One , and started rolling out subscription bundles to users globally. Meta One now has 15 million subscribers. Since Muse is very compute intensive to run, Meta is also building out capacity to expand the AI agent to more than a billion users over the next few years. "We expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale," Zuckerberg said. "If compute efficiency continues improving quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years," he added. Meta narrowed its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 to $135 billion to $145 billion , from its prior range of $130 billion to $145 billion. Muse central to business model of smart glasses Muse is also central to Meta’s plan to build a software and superintelligence business around its smart glasses, which Zuckerberg said are priced to keep hardware profits low. He expects growing sales and paid subscriptions to significantly improve the business’s profitability. Meta expects Reality Labs, the unit which makes smart glasses and VR devices, to narrow losses from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year. For the third quarter, the unit reported an operating loss of $4.13 billion against revenues of $443 million. Overall, Meta's revenues rose 26 percent year-on-year to $64.6 billion while net profit increased 264 percent to $9.86 billion. The net profit was significantly lower than investor expectations, dragged down by a $9.9 billion legal charge related to the settlement of teen mental health and social media lawsuits with nearly all US states in August. Yesterday, a US state court judge ruled that Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The social media giant said it is also creating a new class of non-voting shares with an effective date of January 2027, to help fund its massive AI spending. The move would help the company finance potential acquisitions and attract top talent without diluting voting control of Zuckerberg or other shareholders. "The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said.

extraction.body: The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites. Governments and some of the world's biggest companies are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws. A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a statement. , external Amazon said its threat intelligence system identified it was targeted on Saturday. It added there were further "exploitation attempts" once the embargo on the flaw warning was lifted. The company said it "automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability." When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web. Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites. As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like." Why have websites around the world been taken down? BBC explains Cyber security researcher Ryan Austin, who has been researching PHP security for the last 20 years, said he discovered the flaw in the programming language. He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI". Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October. In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said. The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said. In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said. The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning. The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added. The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days". She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said. The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade. Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure. The websites for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors are currently inaccessible. They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it had followed guidance to take its website offline, "in view of the critical security issues affecting PHP". Edinburgh and Oxford council websites also went offline on Wednesday, but are now accessible. What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble? The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website. This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed. The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database". It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update. passages: When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.
It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.
It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.
E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue.
It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability.
The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.
Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily.
Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.
But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.
Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.

extraction.body: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily. Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs. When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide. The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker". Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts. E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability. The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz. The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can. "Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said. "The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said. Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale. The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post. The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure. "Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre. Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP. The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said. The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors. "Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said. The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

extraction.body: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily. Short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, it powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs. When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide. The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker". Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts. E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability. The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz. The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can. "Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said. "The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said. Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale. The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post. The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure. "Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre. Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP. The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said. The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors. "Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said. The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.

passages: The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites.
What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?

What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?

extraction.body: The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites. Governments and some of the world's biggest companies, including Amazon, are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws. The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them. Amazon was targeted in multiple attempts, which it said occurred before an embargo on the warning was lifted. It added that it was unclear how actors knew about the vulnerabilities. A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note . PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs. When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web. Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October. In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said. The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said. While the PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch", details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday. In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said. The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning. The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added. The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days". She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said. The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade. Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure. What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble? The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website. This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed. The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database". It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update. OpenAI called the discovery, "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". sources.title: Legora reaches $5.55 billion valuation as AI legal tech boom endures - Yahoo Finance
passages: Legora , an AI platform for lawyers, is now valued at $5.55 billion following a $550 million Series D set to fuel its growth in the U.S.
That's despite growing competition with rival Harvey , but also with Microsoft Copilot and generalist large language models (LLMs).
Publicly listed legal software companies saw their stocks drop when Anthropic unveiled a legal plug-in for Claude .
There are other signs that investors are bullish about AI legal tech.
According to Dealroom , they are also on almost identical trajectories with regard to revenue.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
With a focus on embedding itself into its clients' workflows, Legora's platform is now used by 800 law firms and legal teams — and investors took note.

Its Series D was led by Accel, with participation from existing investors Benchmark, Bessemer, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Redpoint Ventures, and Y Combinator; and new backers including Alkeon Capital, Bain Capital, Firstmark Capital, Menlo Ventures, Salesforce Ventures, Sands Capital, and Starwood Capital.
In addition to New York and Stockholm, Legora has offices in Bangalore, London, and Sydney, with more to follow.
Legora is built on top of LLMs, and mostly on Claude , but its positioning as a platform that supports lawyers with complex cases gives CEO Max Junestrand some peace of mind.
"It's amazing that everybody can have their own pocket lawyer in Claude, but we're not solving for the same use case," he said via livestream at the TechArena conference in Stockholm.
Both are also branching out globally; Harvey is pushing hard into Europe , and Legora in the opposite direction.
Formerly known as Judilica, then Leya , the startup is an alum of Stockholm's SSE Business Lab, a known breeding ground for unicorns .

extraction.body: Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion. The company helps automate and assist with workflow tasks for legal professionals, as the industry moves beyond AI assistants to AI services that help them get work done. The news comes just a month after Harvey, Legora’s biggest competitor, announced a $550 million raise at a $15.5 billion valuation; back in March, Harvey also said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was more than $ 200 million. Legora’s Series E follows the company’s April announcement of a $50 million extension of a $550 million Series D round, which valued the company at $5.6 billion. At the time, the company said its ARR had reached $100 million. That number now stands at over $200 million, the company shared on Wednesday. Investors in the latest financing include Atreides Management, which led the round, as well as Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo, and other top names. The company plans to use the fresh capital to further expand across North America. passages: In-house legal teams, which represented only a small fraction of Legora’s customer base a year ago, made up 40% of the company’s new customers in the third quarter.
Stockholm-based legal artificial intelligence startup Legora AB today announced it has raised a notable $550 million in late-stage funding at an $8.8 billion post-money valuation.
Legora provides legal AI agents as teams are beginning to move beyond simple assistants for legal work and into full-service automation that carry out multistep work.
The firm said it is expanding its geographic footprint and offering to capture this hungry market.
Founded in 2023, Legora launched its platform in October 2024.
“Legal is a sophisticated market with demanding buyers, and the bar for software is high,” said Atreides Management LP Chief Information Officer and Managing Partner Gavin Baker.

The company said the capital will support continued global expansion, including in North America, where Legora has offices in New York, Denver, Chicago, Houston, San Francisco, Toronto and Mexico City, as well as in its markets across Europe and Asia-Pacific.

Firms like Legora exist in a space where it assists with less manual production, more technology-supported workflows, greater client pressure on pricing and a premium on verification and legal judgment.

extraction.body: Stockholm-based legal artificial intelligence startup Legora AB today announced it has raised a notable $550 million in late-stage funding at an $8.8 billion post-money valuation. Atreides Management led the Series E round, which also brought participation from new investors Baron Capital, Capital Group, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Glade Brook Capital Partners and J.P. Morgan. Every major existing investor also participated, including Accel, Benchmark, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, ICONIQ, Insight Venture Partners, Redpoint Ventures, Salesforce Ventures and Sands Capital. The round follows the company’s $550 Series D round in March and brings total funding to a staggering $866 million across eight rounds. The company said it has seen a surge in annual recurring revenue from $1 million to $100 million in less than 18 months, faster than any other enterprise software company selling through a direct sales team. The next $100 million took less than six months. Current ARR stands at more than $200 million. Legora provides legal AI agents as teams are beginning to move beyond simple assistants for legal work and into full-service automation that carry out multistep work. The firm said it is expanding its geographic footprint and offering to capture this hungry market. In-house legal teams, which represented only a small fraction of Legora’s customer base a year ago, made up 40% of the company’s new customers in the third quarter. In the United States, Legora’s largest market by revenue is now represented by more than half of AmLaw 50 customers and the company opened its first U.S. office in spring 2025. “The opportunity in legal is enormous and we are still early,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Max Junestrand. “AI is changing the role of the lawyer, with more time for judgment and advice, and it is reshaping how law firms and in-house legal teams are organized and how their work gets done.” Junestrand added that the company intends to lead that shift in the U.S. and globally. Founded in 2023, Legora launched its platform in October 2024. It now has more than 1,000 employees across 18 offices and supports more than 140,000 legal professionals at more than 2,400 leading law firms and in-house legal teams across 80 markets. AI is reshaping the legal industry. It is accelerating research and document work, changing how firms staff and price matters, and enabling corporate legal teams to handle more work internally. The central shift has moved toward the time spent on producing legal work and the judgment applied to work increasingly assisted by software. The transition is underway, but incomplete. Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Ltd. found that 96% of surveyed legal leaders expected technology and AI literacy to grow in importance for in-house lawyers, while 84% of organizations had not yet redesigned roles around AI. Of those surveyed, 61% of departments are now deploying AI, with only 10% with AI fully embedded in workflows. “Legal is a sophisticated market with demanding buyers, and the bar for software is high,” said Atreides Management LP Chief Information Officer and Managing Partner Gavin Baker. “Legora has become the platform that law firms and in-house legal teams adopt and then expand across their organizations, and it has done so while growing at remarkable speed.” Firms like Legora exist in a space where it assists with less manual production, more technology-supported workflows, greater client pressure on pricing and a premium on verification and legal judgment. The company said the capital will support continued global expansion, including in North America, where Legora has offices in New York, Denver, Chicago, Houston, San Francisco, Toronto and Mexico City, as well as in its markets across Europe and Asia-Pacific. It will also deepen investments in its agentic AI legal “operating system,” aOS, bringing in new products to assist lawyers in their work.
