extraction.body: Home Australian Outlook Blog Posts Analysis What Does AUKUS Actually Represent for Australia and the UK? AUKUS promised Australia nuclear-powered submarines and the UK thousands of new jobs. Five years on, as rising costs, workforce shortages and an unpredictable Washington test what’s at stake for both countries. The world is in a very different state than it was when AUKUS was initially announced on September 15th, 2021. In brief, AUKUS is the trilateral security partnership between Australia, the UK and the US focused on advanced defence technology and capability sharing. It achieves this through two ‘pillars’; Pillar 1 focuses on providing nuclear-propelled submarines to Australia through the sale of US Virginia-class submarines to Australia and the building of the new SSN-AUKUS class submarines by Australia and the UK, and Pillar 2 focuses on advanced defence capabilities across various technology areas, including quantum, cyber and AI. To explore the impact of AUKUS on the Australia-UK relationship, the Australia and UK chapters of Women in International Security (WIIS) will co-host a webinar on November 23 rd , 7:30pm AEDT/8:30am GMT. Experts from both countries will explore key areas to watch to ensure AUKUS delivers on its initial promise for both Australia and the UK. For some easy homework, this article provides some explainers of how the UK and Australia are dealing with the implications of AUKUS. Nuclear energy comes from either splitting heavy atomic nuclei (known as fission) or combining light atomic nuclei (known as fusion). Fission is typically carried out with enriched uranium or plutonium. Fission powers nuclear reactors for many purposes, including research, medicine, electricity generation, and propulsion. Six countries currently operate nuclear-propelled submarines, all using enriched uranium: the United States, France, India, China, Russia, and the United Kingdom. AUKUS will make Australia the seventh country in the world. Brazil also has a nuclear-powered submarine program in the works, and South Korea has recently expressed significant interest in it as well. Importantly, nuclear-powered submarines are not the same as nuclear weapons, and Australia remains a non-nuclear-weapon state under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. For navies, nuclear propulsion offers significant advantages. Nuclear-powered submarines can remain submerged for extended periods, travel long distances without refuelling, and operate with greater endurance than conventional submarines. For Australia, whose strategic environment spans vast ocean distances, these capabilities are a central part of the rationale behind acquiring nuclear-powered submarines through AUKUS. UK: Nuclear Energy, Security Partnerships, and AUKUS AUKUS discussions in the UK sit across three live policy discussions: domestic energy policy and security, the UK’s international partnership priorities, and defence spending. For the UK, AUKUS has been framed as supporting Euro-Atlantic security as part of its formal adoption of a ‘NATO first’ defence policy, as well as increased deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. Despite high political leadership turnover in the UK since AUKUS was first signed, there has been broad cross-party support for the partnership, with the Labour government continuing its support following their election in 2024. Domestically, AUKUS has been marketed as a boon for the UK economy, with the recent Geelong treaty valued at up to £20 billion in UK exports over 25 years, and over 7000 new UK jobs . At its peak, 21,000 workers are expected to work on SSN-AUKUS ; however, many of these roles require specialised nuclear skills, highlighting the need for further investment in the UK’s nuclear workforce. There have been calls for an AUKUS Visa, to facilitate the movement of skilled workers and prevent production delays; however, the government has rejected these calls. AUKUS has also been wrapped up in a larger debate on defence spending. In June 2026, the Secretary of State for Defence, John Healey resigned, unable to accept the Defence Investment Plan, referencing the inability to deliver on the Strategic Defence Review. Since then, he has been sworn in as Chancellor of the Exchequer, a signal that the Burnham Government might be looking to prioritising defence spending. A recent House of Commons Defence Committee enquiry found that in the UK AUKUS ‘ has suffered from a lack of meaningful public engagement.’ As the UK factories prepare to ‘cut steel’ in 2027 for the first AUKUS submarine, greater discussion at both the high levels of politics and in the media will be needed to properly scrutinise the partnership, an approach already underway in Australia. For decades, the Australian public has been a staunch voice on the side of nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament, and governments in charge have therefore typically not broached nuclear propulsion as a serious policy point. AUKUS is therefore an outlier in this general attitude. Concerns of capability gaps started seriously emerging in the early 2010’s as the Collins-class submarines currently in use started aging and by 2016 Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull had approached the French to create a new conventionally powered submarine. As part of his announcement of the AUKUS deal in 2021, PM Scott Morrison cancelled the French submarine contract, marketing AUKUS as a better fit for the Australian strategic theatre. The agreement was also presented as part of a broader response to deterioration in the Indo-Pacific security environment. Rather than being solely a submarine acquisition project, AUKUS was framed as a long-term strategic partnership designed to deepen both deterrence and cooperation amongst Australia, the United States, and the United Kingdom. However, the domestic conversation around AUKUS consistently returns to one key point, that being that the deal reinforces Australia’s reliance on its traditional partners, particularly reinforcing its dependence on the US for military support. Debate around the financial strains and the length of time it will take for both Australia and the UK to truly benefit from AUKUS have only exacerbated in response to the US’s pattern of engagement since the return of Trump to office. Five years on from the initial announcement, dissident voices across both nations highlight that the success of the deal requires “heroic optimism.” But the trade-offs that exist for either Australia or the UK to pursue alternatives to AUKUS – including suggestions to cancel the development of the SSN-AUKUS class submarines – are particularly difficult to navigate for policymakers in this era of geopolitics. Neither nation can afford to totally let go of AUKUS and its promise of increased defence capabilities or increased cooperation with allegedly staunch allies when the world order appears unstable. Nina Lopez is currently an Events Officer with Women in International Security – Australia and the Australia–Latin America Emerging Leaders Dialogue. She holds a Master of International Relations from the University of Melbourne, with academic and research interests spanning nuclear security, the role of intelligence in international affairs, the inclusion of marginalised voices in post-conflict justice processes, and Australia’s diplomatic engagement with Latin America. She previously completed a year-long internship with the Australian Institute of International Affairs Victoria, where she supported the coordination and delivery of numerous events and initiatives, including the 2025 International Careers Conference. This blog is part of a joint series between AIIA and WIIS-A, which aims to elevate the work of female and gender-diverse individuals in the field of international affairs. This article is published under a Creative Commons License and may be republished with attribution. If you want to be part of the conversation as WIIS-A and WIIS-UK take on the task of exploring AUKUS in depth through the lens of the UK-Australia relationship, please join them on November 23rd for their WIIS-A x WIIS-UK ‘AUKUS 101’ webinar. AUKUS promised Australia nuclear-powered submarines and the UK thousands of new jobs. Five years on, as rising costs, workforce shortages and an unpredictable Washington test what’s at stake for both countries.

The world is in a very different state than it was when AUKUS was initially announced on September 15th, 2021. In brief, AUKUS is the trilateral security partnership between Australia, the UK and the US focused on advanced defence technology and capability sharing. It achieves this through two ‘pillars’; Pillar 1 focuses on providing nuclear-propelled submarines to Australia through the sale of US Virginia-class submarines to Australia and the building of the new SSN-AUKUS class submarines by Australia and the UK, and Pillar 2 focuses on advanced defence capabilities across various technology areas, including quantum, cyber and AI.

To explore the impact of AUKUS on the Australia-UK relationship, the Australia and UK chapters of Women in International Security (WIIS) will co-host a webinar on November 23 rd , 7:30pm AEDT/8:30am GMT. Experts from both countries will explore key areas to watch to ensure AUKUS delivers on its initial promise for both Australia and the UK. For some easy homework, this article provides some explainers of how the UK and Australia are dealing with the implications of AUKUS.

Nuclear energy comes from either splitting heavy atomic nuclei (known as fission) or combining light atomic nuclei (known as fusion). Fission is typically carried out with enriched uranium or plutonium. Fission powers nuclear reactors for many purposes, including research, medicine, electricity generation, and propulsion. Six countries currently operate nuclear-propelled submarines, all using enriched uranium: the United States, France, India, China, Russia, and the United Kingdom. AUKUS will make Australia the seventh country in the world. Brazil also has a nuclear-powered submarine program in the works, and South Korea has recently expressed significant interest in it as well. Importantly, nuclear-powered submarines are not the same as nuclear weapons, and Australia remains a non-nuclear-weapon state under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

For navies, nuclear propulsion offers significant advantages. Nuclear-powered submarines can remain submerged for extended periods, travel long distances without refuelling, and operate with greater endurance than conventional submarines. For Australia, whose strategic environment spans vast ocean distances, these capabilities are a central part of the rationale behind acquiring nuclear-powered submarines through AUKUS.
UK: Nuclear Energy, Security Partnerships, and AUKUS
AUKUS discussions in the UK sit across three live policy discussions: domestic energy policy and security, the UK’s international partnership priorities, and defence spending.

For the UK, AUKUS has been framed as supporting Euro-Atlantic security as part of its formal adoption of a ‘NATO first’ defence policy, as well as increased deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. Despite high political leadership turnover in the UK since AUKUS was first signed, there has been broad cross-party support for the partnership, with the Labour government continuing its support following their election in 2024.

Domestically, AUKUS has been marketed as a boon for the UK economy, with the recent Geelong treaty valued at up to £20 billion in UK exports over 25 years, and over 7000 new UK jobs . At its peak, 21,000 workers are expected to work on SSN-AUKUS ; however, many of these roles require specialised nuclear skills, highlighting the need for further investment in the UK’s nuclear workforce. There have been calls for an AUKUS Visa, to facilitate the movement of skilled workers and prevent production delays; however, the government has rejected these calls.

AUKUS has also been wrapped up in a larger debate on defence spending. In June 2026, the Secretary of State for Defence, John Healey resigned, unable to accept the Defence Investment Plan, referencing the inability to deliver on the Strategic Defence Review. Since then, he has been sworn in as Chancellor of the Exchequer, a signal that the Burnham Government might be looking to prioritising defence spending.

A recent House of Commons Defence Committee enquiry found that in the UK AUKUS ‘ has suffered from a lack of meaningful public engagement.’ As the UK factories prepare to ‘cut steel’ in 2027 for the first AUKUS submarine, greater discussion at both the high levels of politics and in the media will be needed to properly scrutinise the partnership, an approach already underway in Australia.

For decades, the Australian public has been a staunch voice on the side of nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament, and governments in charge have therefore typically not broached nuclear propulsion as a serious policy point. AUKUS is therefore an outlier in this general attitude. Concerns of capability gaps started seriously emerging in the early 2010’s as the Collins-class submarines currently in use started aging and by 2016 Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull had approached the French to create a new conventionally powered submarine.

As part of his announcement of the AUKUS deal in 2021, PM Scott Morrison cancelled the French submarine contract, marketing AUKUS as a better fit for the Australian strategic theatre. The agreement was also presented as part of a broader response to deterioration in the Indo-Pacific security environment. Rather than being solely a submarine acquisition project, AUKUS was framed as a long-term strategic partnership designed to deepen both deterrence and cooperation amongst Australia, the United States, and the United Kingdom.

However, the domestic conversation around AUKUS consistently returns to one key point, that being that the deal reinforces Australia’s reliance on its traditional partners, particularly reinforcing its dependence on the US for military support.

Debate around the financial strains and the length of time it will take for both Australia and the UK to truly benefit from AUKUS have only exacerbated in response to the US’s pattern of engagement since the return of Trump to office. Five years on from the initial announcement, dissident voices across both nations highlight that the success of the deal requires “heroic optimism.” But the trade-offs that exist for either Australia or the UK to pursue alternatives to AUKUS – including suggestions to cancel the development of the SSN-AUKUS class submarines – are particularly difficult to navigate for policymakers in this era of geopolitics. Neither nation can afford to totally let go of AUKUS and its promise of increased defence capabilities or increased cooperation with allegedly staunch allies when the world order appears unstable.

sources.title: Amazon blocks agentic AI shopping. But Walmart is betting big that it's worth saying yes. - Yahoo Finance
passages: Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy.
The e-commerce giant has blocked Muse from making purchases on its site and prohibits other companies from deploying automated tools to shop.

While Amazon may not be losing much in the way of actual sales — since most people are using AI tools to research rather than to swipe the credit card, so to speak — Walmart is trying to get in early, while habits are still forming.
But in the event that more people delegate their shopping to AI agents, Walmart, and its open embrace of AI partnerships, stands to win.

They cite Walmart's integration with multiple AI ecosystems; the development of the retailer's own shopping assistant named "Sparky"; and its partnerships with other agents, including Meta's Muse, as reasons for Walmart's solid positioning.
Still, Walmart's management team, like everyone else, can't say for certain how popular shopping agents will become.
No doubt there are a number of reasons to block largely untested agents from inserting themselves into your business funnel.

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Americans like to shop. For a lot of consumers, the act of browsing and filling a digital or physical cart isn't a point of friction but a way of life — just ask Costco influencers. But in the event that more people delegate their shopping to AI agents, Walmart, and its open embrace of AI partnerships, stands to win. That's the takeaway in a new note by Bank of America analysts led by Christopher Nardone, published Monday. They cite Walmart's integration with multiple AI ecosystems; the development of the retailer's own shopping assistant named "Sparky"; and its partnerships with other agents, including Meta's Muse, as reasons for Walmart's solid positioning. Walmart is among the key corporate players partnering with Muse , including Best Buy ( BBY ) and Ulta ( ULTA ). These companies are attempting to embrace new modes of digital commerce. Other retailers have taken an antagonistic approach , choosing to block Muse from interacting with their commercial portals. extraction.body: Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers. The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do. With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified and you can cap their spending. The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers.
Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others.
Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended.

That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent.

To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits.
You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time.
Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary.

extraction.body: Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers. The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do. With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified and you can cap their spending. The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site. The company has an important economic moat in reusable rockets, which have made it much less expensive to launch payloads into orbit. That edge helped SpaceX build Starlink, the world's largest satellite internet service. CEO Elon Musk wants to combine those proficiencies to build orbital (space-based) data centers, which could theoretically solve the power and cooling challenges associated with terrestrial data centers. I think investors who are confident in the company's growth prospects can buy a few shares today, but I would keep the position small. Intel is the leader in central processing units (CPUs), with about 59% of the personal computer market and 54% of the data center server market as of the second quarter. However, Intel's impressive financial results say more about the strong demand for CPUs than about the company itself. Despite reporting its best revenue growth in years, Intel still ceded CPU market share to AMD and Arm in PCs and servers in the second quarter. Also, Intel's growth prospects in the foundry space remain questionable, as TSMC dominates the market. Intel currently trades at 87 times adjusted earnings. That seemingly rich figure looks a little more palatable in context. Wall Street expects adjusted earnings to grow at 56% annually through 2027. extraction.body: Billionaire Peter Thiel, a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and entrepreneur, is best known for his role in co-founding Palantir Technologies . He still owns more than 3% of the company's Class A shares, as well as 30% of the Class B shares and 33% of the Class F shares. Thiel also runs a hedge fund, Thiel Macro, that manages $74 million. He made some interesting trades in the third quarter. First, he sold shares of Nvidia and Tesla , closing his position in the former, and trimming his position in the latter. Second, he added shares of Apple ( AAPL +1.32% ) and Microsoft ( MSFT +0.20% ) Those two artificial intelligence (AI) stocks account for 61% of the hedge fund's assets: 27% in Apple and 34% in Microsoft. Of course, the portfolio itself represents a microscopic percentage of Thiel's $26 billion net worth, but the position sizing still points to high conviction in both companies. Apple has cultivated a reputation for premium consumer electronics devices because of design expertise that spans hardware, software, and services. Particularly important is its ability to design custom semiconductors , which improve performance and power efficiency of its iPhone, iPad, and Mac products, and help the company control costs. Apple reported strong financial results in the first quarter of fiscal 2026 (ended Dec. 27), beating estimates on the top and bottom lines. Revenue increased 16% to $143.7 billion despite tariffs, driven by strong growth in the iPhone and services segments. Also, sales in China increased 38% after declining during the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, GAAP net income increased 18% to $2.84 per diluted share. Recently, Apple said it will use Alphabet 's Gemini models to bring artificial intelligence (AI) features to its voice assistant Siri, abandoning plans to build the large language models in house. While that strategy shows Apple's limitations where AI innovation is concerned, it should allow the company to monetize AI more effectively, potentially driving sales growth in the services segment. In late 2024, Apple introduced a suite of generative AI features for new iPhones and Macs. Those capabilities, called Apple Intelligence, are currently free. But the company plans to add a premium version in the next few years, according to Bloomberg . The partnership with Alphabet could prove instrumental in enhancing Apple Intelligence features beyond Siri. However, Apple stock is expensive. Its present valuation of 33 times earnings is quite rich for a company whose earnings are projected to increase at 10% annually over the next three years. For that reason, I would avoid this stock until the price is more reasonable. Microsoft is exploiting is position as the largest enterprise software company to monetize generative AI copilots, conversational assistants integrated into applications for office productivity, enterprise resource planning, and business intelligence. CEO Satya Nadella said copilot seats increased 160% in the most recent quarter, and the number of daily active users increased tenfold. Also, Microsoft doubled down on its status as the IT backbone for most companies with the recent launch of Agent 365, a tool that lets clients manage generative AI agents whether they were built with Microsoft Copilot Studio or developed by partners such as Adobe and ServiceNow . CEO Satya Nadella told analysts, "We are the first provider to offer this type of agent control plane across clouds." Beyond software, Microsoft Azure is exploiting its status as the second largest public cloud to monetize AI. In 2024, the company consolidated its AI services and models into a single platform called Foundry, which lets developers build, customize, test, and manage their AI applications. The number of customers spending at least $1 million per quarter of Foundry increased 80% in the December quarter. In addition, Microsoft owns a 27% equity stake in OpenAI and exclusive rights to its most advanced models, including those that power ChatGPT . That means developers must use Azure (or work directly with OpenAI) if they want to incorporate those models into custom applications. Microsoft wins either way. OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft, according to The Information. Microsoft stock fell 10% after the company delivered disappointing financial results for the December quarter. Capital expenditures related to AI infrastructure exceeded Wall Street's expectations, yet Azure revenue grew more slowly than anticipated. But the selling seems overdone. Microsoft's adjusted earnings increased 24%, which makes the current valuation of 27 times earnings look quite reasonable. Patient investors should consider purchasing a small position. passages: Billionaire Peter Thiel, a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and entrepreneur, is best known for his role in co-founding Palantir Technologies . He still owns more than 3% of the company's Class A shares, as well as 30% of the Class B shares and 33% of the Class F shares.

Thiel also runs a hedge fund, Thiel Macro, that manages $74 million. He made some interesting trades in the third quarter. First, he sold shares of Nvidia and Tesla , closing his position in the former, and trimming his position in the latter. Second, he added shares of Apple ( AAPL +1.32% ) and Microsoft ( MSFT +0.20% )

Those two artificial intelligence (AI) stocks account for 61% of the hedge fund's assets: 27% in Apple and 34% in Microsoft. Of course, the portfolio itself represents a microscopic percentage of Thiel's $26 billion net worth, but the position sizing still points to high conviction in both companies.

Apple has cultivated a reputation for premium consumer electronics devices because of design expertise that spans hardware, software, and services. Particularly important is its ability to design custom semiconductors , which improve performance and power efficiency of its iPhone, iPad, and Mac products, and help the company control costs.

Apple reported strong financial results in the first quarter of fiscal 2026 (ended Dec. 27), beating estimates on the top and bottom lines. Revenue increased 16% to $143.7 billion despite tariffs, driven by strong growth in the iPhone and services segments. Also, sales in China increased 38% after declining during the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, GAAP net income increased 18% to $2.84 per diluted share.

Recently, Apple said it will use Alphabet 's Gemini models to bring artificial intelligence (AI) features to its voice assistant Siri, abandoning plans to build the large language models in house. While that strategy shows Apple's limitations where AI innovation is concerned, it should allow the company to monetize AI more effectively, potentially driving sales growth in the services segment.

In late 2024, Apple introduced a suite of generative AI features for new iPhones and Macs. Those capabilities, called Apple Intelligence, are currently free. But the company plans to add a premium version in the next few years, according to Bloomberg . The partnership with Alphabet could prove instrumental in enhancing Apple Intelligence features beyond Siri.

However, Apple stock is expensive. Its present valuation of 33 times earnings is quite rich for a company whose earnings are projected to increase at 10% annually over the next three years. For that reason, I would avoid this stock until the price is more reasonable.

Microsoft is exploiting is position as the largest enterprise software company to monetize generative AI copilots, conversational assistants integrated into applications for office productivity, enterprise resource planning, and business intelligence. CEO Satya Nadella said copilot seats increased 160% in the most recent quarter, and the number of daily active users increased tenfold.

Also, Microsoft doubled down on its status as the IT backbone for most companies with the recent launch of Agent 365, a tool that lets clients manage generative AI agents whether they were built with Microsoft Copilot Studio or developed by partners such as Adobe and ServiceNow . CEO Satya Nadella told analysts, "We are the first provider to offer this type of agent control plane across clouds."

Beyond software, Microsoft Azure is exploiting its status as the second largest public cloud to monetize AI. In 2024, the company consolidated its AI services and models into a single platform called Foundry, which lets developers build, customize, test, and manage their AI applications. The number of customers spending at least $1 million per quarter of Foundry increased 80% in the December quarter.

In addition, Microsoft owns a 27% equity stake in OpenAI and exclusive rights to its most advanced models, including those that power ChatGPT . That means developers must use Azure (or work directly with OpenAI) if they want to incorporate those models into custom applications. Microsoft wins either way. OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft, according to The Information.

Microsoft stock fell 10% after the company delivered disappointing financial results for the December quarter. Capital expenditures related to AI infrastructure exceeded Wall Street's expectations, yet Azure revenue grew more slowly than anticipated. But the selling seems overdone. Microsoft's adjusted earnings increased 24%, which makes the current valuation of 27 times earnings look quite reasonable. Patient investors should consider purchasing a small position.

Investors withdrew a staggering $487 million from U.S. spot Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) ETFs on October 7, 2026, followed by another $244 million on October 8.
These two days marked the highest Bitcoin ETF outflows of the week.
A spot Bitcoin ETF , also known as an exchange-traded fund, directly holds Bitcoin and trades on stock exchanges, allowing investors to purchase Bitcoin through their regular brokerage accounts.
Ethereum ETFs , the second-largest group, faced losses throughout the week, totaling around $542 million.
Their worst day was October 6, when $202 million exited, even as Bitcoin ETFs attracted buyers.
This marks nine consecutive days of outflows for Ethereum, with the last positive inflow occurring on September 28, when $17.1 million entered the fund.
This small gain barely recovers 3% of what was withdrawn, and the funds’ total assets ended the week lower than where they started.
Nevertheless, this positive trend did not extend to other funds.
That same day, Ethereum ETFs lost $56 million, while Solana ETFs fell $3.8 million.
However, on October 9, these Bitcoin funds experienced a positive shift, attracting $21 million in inflows—their first increase since October 6.
Bitcoin ETFs remain the largest category in the crypto fund space, shifting direction three times over five sessions.
Despite a rough week, Bitcoin ETFs have still drawn a remarkable $57.1 billion in net inflows since their inception, showing strong overall investor interest.
If Ethereum ETFs record their first inflow since September 28, coupled with a second consecutive inflow for Bitcoin ETFs, it would signal easing selling pressure.
Bitcoin ETF net assets, which reflect the total dollar value these funds hold, tell a more complex story.
Similarly, Solana ETFs experienced minor losses every day, with five straight sessions of outflows since their last inflow on October 2.
The steady decline of around $25 million suggests a slow trim of investments rather than a panic sell-off.
They brought in $11.3 million over two sessions while remaining stable on the other three days.
While Bitcoin and Ethereum funds hemorrhage hundreds of millions, XRP funds are quietly pulling in new money from investors already sitting on heavy losses.
U.S. investors pulled money from Solana ETFs for seven of eight straight trading sessions in October, yet a Hong Kong asset manager chose that exact moment to launch a brand-new spot Solana fund.
Billions poured into Bitcoin funds throughout September, then something shifted on the very last trading day of the quarter.

Investors withdrew a staggering $487 million from U.S. spot Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) ETFs on October 7, 2026, followed by another $244 million on October 8.
These two days marked the highest Bitcoin ETF outflows of the week.
A spot Bitcoin ETF , also known as an exchange-traded fund, directly holds Bitcoin and trades on stock exchanges, allowing investors to purchase Bitcoin through their regular brokerage accounts.
Ethereum ETFs , the second-largest group, faced losses throughout the week, totaling around $542 million.
Their worst day was October 6, when $202 million exited, even as Bitcoin ETFs attracted buyers.
This marks nine consecutive days of outflows for Ethereum, with the last positive inflow occurring on September 28, when $17.1 million entered the fund.
This small gain barely recovers 3% of what was withdrawn, and the funds’ total assets ended the week lower than where they started.
Nevertheless, this positive trend did not extend to other funds.
That same day, Ethereum ETFs lost $56 million, while Solana ETFs fell $3.8 million.
However, on October 9, these Bitcoin funds experienced a positive shift, attracting $21 million in inflows—their first increase since October 6.
Bitcoin ETFs remain the largest category in the crypto fund space, shifting direction three times over five sessions.
Despite a rough week, Bitcoin ETFs have still drawn a remarkable $57.1 billion in net inflows since their inception, showing strong overall investor interest.
If Ethereum ETFs record their first inflow since September 28, coupled with a second consecutive inflow for Bitcoin ETFs, it would signal easing selling pressure.
Bitcoin ETF net assets, which reflect the total dollar value these funds hold, tell a more complex story.
Similarly, Solana ETFs experienced minor losses every day, with five straight sessions of outflows since their last inflow on October 2.
The steady decline of around $25 million suggests a slow trim of investments rather than a panic sell-off.
They brought in $11.3 million over two sessions while remaining stable on the other three days.
While Bitcoin and Ethereum funds hemorrhage hundreds of millions, XRP funds are quietly pulling in new money from investors already sitting on heavy losses.
U.S. investors pulled money from Solana ETFs for seven of eight straight trading sessions in October, yet a Hong Kong asset manager chose that exact moment to launch a brand-new spot Solana fund.
Billions poured into Bitcoin funds throughout September, then something shifted on the very last trading day of the quarter.

That’s according to the company’s third-quarter earnings report released on Wednesday, which says Meta’s income from operations would have been $22.89 billion without the settlement.
It will also only pay $5.3 billion of this amount if YouTube and TikTok implement stricter settings and safeguards for kids, which Meta also agreed to as part of the settlement.
Even with the fees associated with its legal battles, Meta reported earning $64.60 billion in revenue, marking a 26 percent increase from the same time last year.

extraction.body: Survey of 2,018 IT heads at big firms points to a lack of leverage. Enterprise-sized businesses spend, on average, 28 percent of their software budgets on unwanted upgrades, migrations, and licensing changes. Often, those firms’ IT heads think those changes are detrimental. Those results are according to a survey of 2,018 chief information officers and senior IT decision-makers at companies with at least 10,000 employees that Origina commissioned for its report, “ The Software Tax .” About half of the respondents (1,011) are from the US, and the rest are from the United Kingdom. All respondents worked at companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Keep in mind that Origina provides maintenance for various enterprise software. Its report points to independent software maintenance as a way for IT leaders to regain control over software budgets, illustrating its potential bias. A third-party research consultancy, Censuswide , conducted the survey. Among the report’s most concerning findings, enterprises often make software purchases that IT heads believe could hurt the organization. Ninety-five percent of respondents said “their organization has paid for a vendor-driven upgrade, migration, or licensing change in the past three years that it believed at the time would reduce performance, reliability, or business value,” the report says. Fifty-three percent of respondents “have done so more than once,” the report notes. “Some 76 percent say their organization has very little real leverage in negotiations, and 80 percent say moving away from major vendors would cause significant disruption,” the report says, referring to the share of respondents who selected “strongly agree” or “somewhat agree” to those statements. “When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response,” Tomás O’Leary, one of the report’s authors and Origina’s CEO and founder, said in a statement. “That’s exactly the problem. The market has left some of the most experienced technology leaders in the world with little room to refuse, and that cost shows up in budgets, in engineering time, and in innovation that never gets funded.” The result is less funding for other areas, particularly, per the report, innovation (named by 36 percent of respondents), human resources (32 percent), security (31 percent), and “customer-facing investment” (31 percent). In a statement accompanying the survey’s announcement, Liberty Mutual’s CIO, James McGlennon, pointed out that an upgrade cycle could occupy top technical workers for “the better part of a year.” “That’s not a one-off cost, it’s a recurring drag on capacity, and every year it repeats is a year those people aren’t working on the initiatives that actually differentiate the business,” he said. The majority (91 percent) surveyed would support laws that give enterprises “protections comparable with those available to long-term residential tenants.” Only 1 percent opposed this (with the rest signaling that they neither support nor oppose the idea). CIOs should “negotiate the exit before the entry” to have more control over software budgets, Marshall Van Alstyne, the report’s co-author and an information sciences professor at Boston University, said in a statement. Origina’s report suggests “settling the terms of a potential exit,” including setting a price for migration assistance and caps on renewal and expansion prices, during initial negotiations with the software vendor. Origina’s report didn’t call out any specific vendors as forcing enterprises’ hands. However, every survey respondent currently runs “at least one of IBM, HCL, VMware/Broadcom, or SAP at meaningful scale.” Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years.
